# AI 3 A 3D Solar System

This notebook is a working 3D model of the Solar System, made from **three prompts** and no hand-written code. The planets are where they really are today (roughly), spin at their real rates, and move as fast as you like.

Each prompt is printed in full above the cell it made, and saved in that cell: press **✨** to open it, change it, and **Replace cell** or **Generate copy**.

Press **Run all**, then drag the scene to look around and click a planet.

## Prompt 1: the facts

> Store accurate data for the Sun, the eight planets and Earth's Moon in nb.bodies, as a list of objects with: name, type ("star", "planet" or "moon"), parent (for the Moon: "Earth"), radius_km, distance_au from the Sun (for the Moon, its distance from Earth in AU), orbital_period_days, rotation_period_hours (negative when the spin is backwards), axial_tilt_deg, longitude_j2000_deg (the planet's mean longitude on 1 January 2000), a hex colour that looks like the real body, and one surprising fact. Then return a tidy HTML table of the planets on a dark card: a colour dot and name, radius, distance from the Sun, the time for one orbit (in days under a year, otherwise years) and the tilt.

Asking for the data in its own cell has two benefits: you can check the numbers in the table, and the 3D cell can be regenerated as often as you like without the facts drifting.

## Prompt 2: the controls

> Controls for a 3D solar system, in one row 900 pixels wide: a slider "Speed" bound to days_per_second (0 to 120, step 1, default 10, suffix " days/s"); checkboxes "Orbits" bound to show_orbits and "Labels" bound to show_labels (both default true); a dropdown "Follow" bound to follow with the options none and each planet's name (default none); and a "Reset view" button with the fa-rotate-left icon that increments reset_view.

## Prompt 3: the scene

> A 3D solar system with three.js that fills its frame and follows it when it resizes (900 by 540 on a desktop; on a narrow phone screen, step the camera back so every orbit stays in view). Load /shared/lib/three/0.128.0/build/three.min.js and /shared/lib/three/0.128.0/examples/js/controls/OrbitControls.js. Read nb.bodies. Put the Sun at the centre as a glowing sphere with a point light, and each planet on a circular orbit, with distances squashed by a square root and sizes enlarged on a log scale so everything is visible. Place every planet at its real position for today's date using longitude_j2000_deg and orbital_period_days, then move time forward by nb.days_per_second. Spin each planet by its rotation period around an axis tilted by axial_tilt_deg. Give the planets simple canvas textures (bands on the gas giants, a red spot on Jupiter, land and ice caps on Earth, blotches on the rocky ones), Saturn a ring, Earth its Moon, and add a field of background stars and an asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Draw orbit lines when nb.show_orbits is on and name labels when nb.show_labels is on. Show the simulated date in the top left. Clicking a planet opens a card with its orbit time, distance, length of one spin (say "backwards" when negative), radius and fact. When nb.follow names a planet, fly the camera in close to it and then travel along with it; when nb.reset_view changes, the camera goes back to its starting view. Read the nb values in a function passed to nb.onChange so the animation never restarts.

This is the prompt that does the heavy lifting, and it's long on purpose. Every sentence is something you'd otherwise have to fix afterwards: where the libraries live, how to keep everything visible, what "today" means, and that changing a control must not restart the animation.

> **How it was steered.** The first version said only *"the camera follows it"*. The model kept the camera where it was and turned it to watch the planet, which was technically following but felt wrong. Changing it to *"fly the camera in close to it and then travel along with it"* gave the close-up you see when you pick a planet under **Follow**.
Drag to turn, scroll to zoom, click a planet for facts

## Make it yours

Press **✨** on the scene and add a sentence, or use **⚡ AI Generate New Cell** for something new:

- *"Add Pluto on its tilted, stretched orbit, and a comet whose tail always points away from the Sun."*
- *"Add a date picker control bound to view_date, and jump the planets to that date when it changes."*
- *"When I click a planet, fly the camera smoothly to it and show its moons."*
- *"Add a toggle for true distances, so I can see how empty space really is."*

The more precisely you say what you want to see and how it should behave, the closer the first try gets.

**Next:** tutorial **AI 4** builds a complete arcade game from prompts.
